extracted.intended_audience: theatre audiences, literature students, and writers interested in Oscar Wilde's wit and comedic technique
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and applying the techniques of Oscar Wilde's epigrams and paradoxical wit to create concise, ironic, and socially unsettling humor. Focuses on phrasing, paradox, allusion, tone, and structural mirroring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obsession with paradox
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde's distinctive style grows out of his obsession with paradox; paradoxes upset the status quo, disrupt the thoughtless cliché, and toy with lionized rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paradox as a primary device to destabilize familiar assumptions; craft statements that invert or undermine conventional wisdom to create intellectual surprise and comic tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epigrams as self-contained works
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde treated epigrams as one-line works of art: 'Words were sacred to him; each word was perfectly placed in the phrase, each phrase linked to the next. Each one-liner was its own work of art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for brevity and meticulous word choice; every word must earn its place. Treat the sentence as a complete artistic unit rather than a throw-away punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion of tone (seriousness vs. triviality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde's stated philosophy: 'We should treat all the trivial things of life very seriously, and all the serious things of life with sincere and studied triviality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invert expected tones: give extravagant seriousness to petty matters and flippancy to solemn subjects to reveal absurdity and provoke thought alongside laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contrast, symmetry, and sound
rubrics_metrics.description: The craft values contrast, symmetry and sound in phrasing (for example: 'He atones for being occasionally somewhat over-dressed, by being always absolutely over-educated.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct lines with parallel structure, balanced contrasts, and attention to rhythm and sonic quality to increase memorability and elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting trite or entrenched ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The best of Wilde's epigrams play directly with trite, entrenched ideas or phrases, upsetting tired conventions of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick well-known platitudes, idioms, or moralistic statements and subvert them—parodying the cliché both exposes and exploits its familiarity for comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextual allusion and literary referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde had an encyclopedic knowledge of literary history and constantly references his artistic heritage for humor and context (e.g. twisting Shakespeare's 'All the world's a stage...' to 'The world is a stage, but the play is badly cast.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical or canonical references as a foil—rework famous lines or ideas so the audience recognizes the echo and appreciates the twist; this leverages shared cultural knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirizing preaching rhetoric and moralistic banalities
rubrics_metrics.description: As an expatriate Irishman, Wilde was intensely suspicious of preaching rhetoric; supposed sincerity and moralistic banalities served as targets (example: 'Work is the curse of the drinking classes.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim humor at sanctimonious or moralizing language—expose performative sincerity by treating its claims with ironic distance or flippant reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical contradiction to provoke uneasy laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde's rhetorical contradiction 'jangles the nerves of an audience' and produces 'laugh[ter] angrily'—the audience is amused while simultaneously irritated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design lines that create cognitive dissonance—make the audience laugh while feeling a provocative tug (anger, discomfort, recognition). This mixture can make humor more cutting and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form mirroring content — structural symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Importance of Being Earnest' is where form finally marries content: the symmetry of phrase matches the harmony of structure; characters and plots mirror each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structure (parallel characters, mirrored scenes, repeated motifs) to reinforce the epigrammatic theme; let plot mechanics reflect the central paradox or aphorism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradoxical reversals where truth dissolves
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde uses contradictory reversals (e.g., Jack's lie about a brother named Ernest is both false and then confirmed true) so that 'truth dissolves' and lies are simultaneously confirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ plot or rhetorical devices that reverse status or meaning, allowing a statement to be both undermined and validated—this generates a satisfying twist that embodies the epigram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and universality of phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde's phrases endure due to their precision and universality; he 'summed up all systems in a phrase, and all existence in an epigram.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for concise lines that capture a broad observation; aim for aphorisms that feel universally resonant while remaining sharply specific in wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intent: pleasure in irritation over didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde enjoyed provoking irritation for its own aesthetic effect rather than as a means to social reform (contrast with Shaw's desire to convert anger into change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your comic aim is to unsettle or to persuade; Wildean wit favors aesthetic provocation and the joy of cleverness over explicit moral instruction.
